# Unit 2: Drug and disease classification, dictionaries and setting up a pharmacovigilance programme

Pharmacovigilance works only if a report written in Ghaziabad means exactly the same as one written in Uppsala or Tokyo. That needs standard ways of naming drugs, diseases and reactions. This unit covers the international classifications of drugs (ATC, DDD, INN) and diseases (ICD), the dictionaries used to code adverse reactions and medicines (WHO-ART, MedDRA, SMQs, WHODrug, EVMPD), where to look for drug safety information, and how a pharmacovigilance programme is set up in a hospital, in a company and in a country.

## 2.1 Why classification and coding matter

| Problem without coding | Result |
| --- | --- |
| One drug sold under hundreds of brand names | Reports on the same drug are scattered |
| Same reaction written as "rash", "skin eruption", "exanthema" | Cases cannot be counted together |
| Different languages and spellings | International data cannot be pooled |
| Free text in databases | Computer searches and signal detection fail |

**Coding** turns free text into standard terms and codes so that cases can be stored, searched, counted, compared and exchanged electronically.

## 2.2 Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification

The **ATC system** classifies active substances by the organ or system on which they act and by their therapeutic, pharmacological and chemical properties. It is maintained by the **WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology, Oslo, Norway**, and is recommended by WHO for drug utilisation research.

**Five levels**

| Level | What it shows | Example: metformin A10BA02 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | Anatomical main group (one letter; 14 groups) | A — Alimentary tract and metabolism |
| 2nd | Therapeutic subgroup (two digits) | A10 — Drugs used in diabetes |
| 3rd | Pharmacological subgroup (letter) | A10B — Blood glucose lowering drugs, excluding insulins |
| 4th | Chemical subgroup (letter) | A10BA — Biguanides |
| 5th | Chemical substance (two digits) | A10BA02 — Metformin |

**The 14 anatomical main groups:** A alimentary tract and metabolism; B blood and blood-forming organs; C cardiovascular system; D dermatologicals; G genito-urinary system and sex hormones; H systemic hormonal preparations (excluding sex hormones and insulins); J anti-infectives for systemic use; L antineoplastic and immunomodulating agents; M musculo-skeletal system; N nervous system; P antiparasitic products, insecticides and repellents; R respiratory system; S sensory organs; V various.

Another example: paracetamol N02BE01 (N nervous system → N02 analgesics → N02B other analgesics and antipyretics → N02BE anilides → paracetamol).

**Principles:** a substance usually gets one ATC code per main indication and route; combinations get separate codes; a code is not a recommendation for use and does not imply therapeutic equivalence.

**Uses in pharmacovigilance:** grouping suspect drugs by class in VigiBase, finding class effects, drug utilisation studies, comparing consumption between countries.

## 2.3 Defined Daily Dose (DDD)

**DDD** is the **assumed average maintenance dose per day for a drug used for its main indication in adults**. It is a **technical unit of measurement**, set by the WHO Oslo centre together with the ATC code. It is **not** a recommended dose and may differ from the dose actually prescribed.

**Common measures**

- **DDDs per 1,000 inhabitants per day** — population consumption:

  ```text
  DDD/1000 inhabitants/day = total quantity used (mg) × 1000
                             ─────────────────────────────────────
                             DDD (mg) × number of days × inhabitants
  ```

- **DDDs per 100 bed-days** — hospital use.
- **DDDs per inhabitant per year** — for drugs used in short courses (for example anti-infectives).

**Uses:** comparing drug use between hospitals, regions and countries over time independent of price and pack size; estimating exposure (the denominator) for ADR rates; studying antibiotic consumption and resistance.

**Limitations:** does not reflect actual prescribed doses (children, renal disease), does not show indication or adherence, combination products are difficult.

## 2.4 International Classification of Diseases (ICD)

The **ICD**, published by WHO, is the global standard for recording diseases, injuries and causes of death.

| Feature | ICD-10 | ICD-11 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status | Endorsed in 1990; widely used, including in Indian hospitals | Adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019; in effect from 1 January 2022 |
| Code format | Letter + digits, e.g. E11 (type 2 diabetes mellitus), I10 (essential hypertension), J45 (asthma) | Alphanumeric codes such as 5A11; electronic, linked to a foundation layer |
| Structure | 22 chapters by body system or cause (the last for special purposes) | More chapters, including new ones such as traditional medicine conditions |

**Uses in PV:** coding the indication and medical history, separating disease symptoms from ADRs, mortality and morbidity statistics, linking hospital records in pharmacoepidemiological studies. ICD also contains codes for adverse effects of drugs in therapeutic use and for poisoning.

## 2.5 International Nonproprietary Names (INN)

An **INN** is a unique, globally recognised generic name for a pharmaceutical substance, selected by WHO through the INN programme (started in 1950). INNs are public property and cannot be registered as trademarks.

**Features**

- Distinctive in sound and spelling, not too long, not confusable with existing names.
- Related substances share a **common stem**, so the name shows the class.

| Stem | Class | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -olol | Beta-blockers | propranolol, atenolol |
| -pril | ACE inhibitors | enalapril, ramipril |
| -sartan | Angiotensin II receptor blockers | losartan, telmisartan |
| -dipine | Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers | amlodipine, nifedipine |
| -statin | HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors | atorvastatin, rosuvastatin |
| -prazole | Proton pump inhibitors | omeprazole, pantoprazole |
| -oxacin | Quinolone antibacterials | ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin |
| -vir | Antivirals | acyclovir, oseltamivir |
| -mab | Monoclonal antibodies | rituximab, trastuzumab |
| -tinib | Tyrosine kinase inhibitors | imatinib, gefitinib |

**Importance for PV:** reports on many brands of one substance can be combined; prescribing and labelling by generic name reduces medication errors; avoids confusion when drugs move between countries.

## 2.6 WHO adverse reaction terminology (WHO-ART)

**WHO-ART** was developed by WHO–UMC to code adverse reaction terms in the WHO programme for several decades.

- Hierarchical: **System Organ Class → High Level Term → Preferred Term → Included Term**.
- Simple, available in several languages, linked to ICD.
- Limitations: relatively small and coarse; not detailed enough for modern regulatory needs.
- It has now largely been **replaced by MedDRA**, which is the standard for ICSRs; WHO–UMC supports MedDRA in VigiBase and VigiFlow.

## 2.7 MedDRA — Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities

**MedDRA** is a clinically validated, international medical terminology developed under **ICH** for regulatory communication about human medicines. It is maintained by the **MSSO (Maintenance and Support Services Organization)**, with new versions released twice a year (March and September). It is used for adverse events, medical history, indications, investigations and product-quality issues, at every stage from clinical trials to post-marketing.

**Five-level hierarchy**

```text
SOC   System Organ Class (27)            e.g. Gastrointestinal disorders
 └ HLGT  High Level Group Term            e.g. Gastrointestinal signs and symptoms
    └ HLT   High Level Term               e.g. Nausea and vomiting symptoms
       └ PT    Preferred Term             e.g. Vomiting
          └ LLT   Lowest Level Term       e.g. Throwing up, Vomiting
```

- **LLT** — the level used for coding; includes synonyms, lexical variants and common words a reporter may use ("throwing up").
- **PT** — a single distinct medical concept; the level used for counting and analysis.
- **Multiaxiality** — a PT may belong to more than one SOC (for example, "pneumonia" relates to infections and to respiratory disorders), but each PT has **one primary SOC** for counting so that cases are not double counted.

**Coding rules (good practice):** code what the reporter says, do not add a diagnosis that was not made; if a diagnosis is given, code the diagnosis rather than every symptom; select the LLT closest to the verbatim term; do not code "unknown" or lazy terms when details exist; record the MedDRA version used.

**Standardised MedDRA Queries (SMQs)** — pre-defined groupings of MedDRA terms (usually PTs) that relate to one medical condition, for example *Rhabdomyolysis/myopathy*, *Severe cutaneous adverse reactions*, *Drug-related hepatic disorders*, *Torsade de pointes/QT prolongation*.

- **Narrow scope** — terms highly likely to represent the condition (specific).
- **Broad scope** — narrow terms plus less specific terms (sensitive).
- Some are **hierarchical** (sub-SMQs) and some **algorithmic** (combinations of terms).
- Use: retrieving all relevant cases from a safety database for signal evaluation and aggregate reports.

## 2.8 WHO Drug Dictionary (WHODrug)

**WHODrug Global** (formerly the WHO Drug Dictionary and WHO Drug Dictionary Enhanced) is the international dictionary of medicinal product information maintained by **WHO–UMC**.

- Contains conventional medicines, biologicals and herbal products from many countries, with trade names, active ingredients, manufacturers and countries.
- Each record has a **drug code** that links trade names to the same active ingredient(s), plus **ATC codes**.
- Herbal products are covered by **WHODrug Herbal**, which uses a herbal ATC (HATC) classification.
- Used for coding **concomitant and suspect medications** in clinical trial databases and ICSRs, and for analysing data by ingredient or class.

## 2.9 EudraVigilance Medicinal Product Dictionary (EVMPD)

**EudraVigilance** is the European Medicines Agency's system for managing ICSRs in the European Economic Area. Its **Medicinal Product Dictionary (EVMPD)**, now the **extended version (xEVMPD)**, holds information on medicines authorised in the EU and on investigational products.

- Marketing authorisation holders must submit and update data on their authorised products (product name, substances, strength, pharmaceutical form, route, MAH, QPPV details).
- Supports accurate identification of products in ICSRs and signal detection.
- Is being aligned with the ISO **IDMP** (Identification of Medicinal Products) standards.

**Comparison of dictionaries**

| Dictionary | Owner / maintainer | Codes what |
| --- | --- | --- |
| WHO-ART | WHO–UMC | Adverse reactions (older) |
| MedDRA | ICH; MSSO | Adverse events, indications, history, investigations |
| WHODrug | WHO–UMC | Medicinal products and ingredients |
| xEVMPD | EMA | EU-authorised and investigational products |
| ICD | WHO | Diseases and causes of death |
| ATC/DDD | WHO Oslo centre | Drug classes and consumption units |

## 2.10 Information resources in pharmacovigilance

**Basic drug information resources**

- Product information: package inserts, summary of product characteristics (SmPC), prescribing information.
- Compendia and formularies: National Formulary of India, Indian Pharmacopoeia, British National Formulary, Martindale, CIMS and similar Indian indexes.
- Standard textbooks of pharmacology and therapeutics.
- Databases: Micromedex, Lexicomp, Medscape, Drugs.com; PubMed for primary literature.

**Specialised resources for ADRs**

| Resource | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Meyler's Side Effects of Drugs and Side Effects of Drugs Annual | Comprehensive reference on reported ADRs |
| Davies's Textbook of Adverse Drug Reactions | Organ-wise ADR information |
| Stockley's Drug Interactions | Interactions |
| Reactions Weekly | Abstracts of new case reports |
| WHO Pharmaceuticals Newsletter, WHO Drug Information | Regulatory safety actions worldwide |
| VigiAccess (WHO), FAERS (USA), EudraVigilance public site, Yellow Card data (UK) | Public views of spontaneous report databases |
| PvPI drug safety alerts and newsletters, CDSCO notices | Indian safety actions |
| LiverTox, LactMed | Drug-induced liver injury; drugs in breastfeeding |
| Briggs' Drugs in Pregnancy and Lactation | Pregnancy and lactation risk |

**Hierarchy of evidence:** tertiary sources (textbooks) for quick answers → secondary (indexing databases) → primary literature (case reports, studies) for new or rare reactions.

## 2.11 Establishing a pharmacovigilance programme in a hospital

**Steps**

1. **Approval and policy** — hospital management and the Pharmacy and Therapeutics Committee approve an ADR monitoring programme; ideally register as or link to a PvPI AMC.
2. **Pharmacovigilance committee** — physicians, pharmacologists, clinical pharmacists, nurses; defines scope and meets regularly.
3. **Responsible staff** — a PV coordinator (often a clinical pharmacist or pharmacologist).
4. **Tools** — PvPI reporting forms in wards, drop boxes, helpline and app information, an ADR register.
5. **Training and awareness** — CMEs, ward rounds, posters; make reporting easy and non-punitive.
6. **Detection methods** — spontaneous reporting plus active methods (ward rounds, trigger tools, review of antidote use and laboratory alerts).
7. **Assessment** — causality (WHO–UMC, Naranjo), severity (Hartwig), preventability (Schumock–Thornton).
8. **Reporting** — forward to AMC/PvPI through VigiFlow.
9. **Feedback and action** — acknowledgement to reporters, bulletins, formulary changes, allergy alert system.
10. **Evaluation** — number and quality of reports, preventable ADRs reduced.

## 2.12 Drug safety department in industry

A **marketing authorisation holder (MAH)** must run a pharmacovigilance system for its products.

**Organisation**

```text
Head of drug safety / Qualified person responsible for PV
        │
 ┌──────┼──────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐
Case     Aggregate      Signal          Risk           Quality,
processing reports      management      management     SOPs, audits
(ICSRs)  (PSUR/PBRER,   (detection,     (RMP,          and training
          DSUR)          evaluation)     minimisation)
```

**Case processing workflow:** case receipt (doctors, patients, literature, partners, social media, trials) → duplicate check → validity check (four minimum criteria) → triage (serious/non-serious, expected/unexpected) → data entry in a safety database → MedDRA and WHODrug coding → medical review and causality → narrative writing → quality check → submission to regulators within timelines → follow-up.

**Other functions:** literature surveillance, maintaining reference safety information, safety data exchange agreements with partners, inspection readiness, PV system master file (where required), training of all staff (including sales staff, who must pass on any ADR they hear about).

## 2.13 Contract Research Organisations (CROs)

A **CRO** is a company contracted by a sponsor to perform trial- or PV-related duties.

- PV services offered: case processing, literature screening, aggregate report writing, signal detection, medical review, call-centre intake.
- The **sponsor/MAH stays legally responsible**; duties are defined in written contracts and agreements.
- Quality is ensured by SOPs, audits, timelines (key performance indicators) and data-protection rules.
- India has a large PV outsourcing industry, which offers careers for B.Pharm graduates as drug safety associates.

## 2.14 Establishing a national pharmacovigilance programme

Basic requirements for a national system:

1. A **national PV centre** with trained staff, an official mandate and stable funding.
2. A **national reporting system** with a standard ICSR form and easy channels (paper, online, app, helpline).
3. A **national database** compatible with international standards (E2B, MedDRA) and links to the WHO programme.
4. An **expert advisory committee** for causality and signal review.
5. A **clear link with the regulator** so that findings lead to action.
6. **Regional/peripheral centres** to collect reports (like AMCs in India).
7. A **communication strategy** for feedback, alerts and public information.
8. Training and promotion of reporting among health professionals and consumers.
9. Collaboration with public health programmes (TB, HIV, malaria, immunisation).

**Phases:** plan and get government support → set up the centre and tools → pilot in a few hospitals → expand nationally → join the WHO programme → integrate with regulatory decisions.

## Remember

- ATC: 5 levels, 14 main groups; WHO Oslo centre. Metformin A10BA02.
- DDD = assumed average maintenance dose per day for the main indication in adults; a measuring unit, not a recommended dose.
- ICD-10 in use; ICD-11 effective 1 January 2022.
- INN stems: -olol, -pril, -sartan, -statin, -mab, -tinib.
- MedDRA: SOC (27) → HLGT → HLT → PT → LLT; code at LLT, analyse at PT; one primary SOC; maintained by MSSO; SMQs narrow and broad.
- WHODrug (WHO–UMC) codes medicines; xEVMPD (EMA) codes EU products; WHO-ART is older and replaced by MedDRA.
- Industry PV: case processing, aggregate reports, signals, RMP; MAH remains responsible even when a CRO does the work.

# Unit 3: Vaccine safety, pharmacovigilance methods and communication

Vaccines are given to healthy people, often children, in huge numbers, so even a rare problem — or a rumour about one — can damage a whole immunisation programme. This unit first covers vaccine pharmacovigilance. It then describes the methods used to collect safety data (passive, stimulated and active surveillance, observational studies and targeted investigations), how signals are found in that data, and finally how safety information is communicated, including during a crisis.

## 3.1 Vaccine pharmacovigilance

**Definition.** Vaccine pharmacovigilance is the science and activities relating to the detection, assessment, understanding and communication of **adverse events following immunisation (AEFI)** and other vaccine- or immunisation-related problems, and their prevention.

**Why vaccines need special attention**

- Given to **healthy** people, often infants and pregnant women, so tolerance of risk is low.
- Given to **very large populations** in campaigns; rare events appear in absolute numbers.
- Many events occur by **coincidence** around the age of vaccination (for example, febrile seizures, sudden infant death).
- Biological products: lot-to-lot variation, cold-chain problems, contamination.
- Public confidence is fragile; a safety scare can cause outbreaks of vaccine-preventable disease.

## 3.2 Adverse events following immunisation (AEFI)

**AEFI** — any untoward medical occurrence which follows immunisation and which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the use of the vaccine. It may be an unfavourable sign, abnormal laboratory finding, symptom or disease.

**Cause-specific classification (WHO/CIOMS)**

| Type | Cause | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vaccine product-related reaction | Inherent property of the vaccine | Fever, local swelling; vaccine-associated paralytic polio after oral polio vaccine; anaphylaxis |
| Vaccine quality defect-related reaction | Manufacturing defect (including the administration device) | Incompletely inactivated vaccine causing infection |
| Immunisation error-related reaction | Inappropriate handling, prescribing or administration — preventable | Abscess from non-sterile injection; toxic shock from a contaminated reconstituted vial; wrong diluent; injection given in the wrong site |
| Immunisation anxiety-related reaction | Fear or pain of injection, not the vaccine | Fainting (vasovagal syncope), hyperventilation, mass psychogenic reactions in schools |
| Coincidental event | Caused by something other than the vaccine or process | An infant with a pre-existing infection who develops fever |

**Seriousness and severity** follow the same logic as for drugs: serious = death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly; severe = intensity.

**Common minor reactions:** pain, redness and swelling at the site, fever, irritability, malaise. **Rare serious reactions:** anaphylaxis, seizures, thrombocytopenia, Guillain–Barré syndrome (reported with some vaccines), intussusception (with some rotavirus vaccines).

**Case definitions.** The **Brighton Collaboration** publishes standard case definitions for AEFIs (for example, anaphylaxis, fever, GBS) with levels of diagnostic certainty, so that reports from different places are comparable.

**AEFI surveillance in India**

- Run under the Universal Immunisation Programme by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, with **district, state and national AEFI committees**.
- Serious AEFIs (deaths, hospitalisations, clusters) are reported promptly and **investigated** by the district team: case details, vaccine and lot, storage, handling, other vaccinees from the same vial.
- Causality is assessed with the **WHO AEFI causality algorithm**, which places a case as **consistent with causal association**, **indeterminate**, **inconsistent** (coincidental) or **unclassifiable**.
- Minor AEFIs are recorded and reported in routine reports; PvPI also accepts vaccine ADR reports.

**Management at the site:** observe vaccinees for about 30 minutes after vaccination; keep an anaphylaxis kit (adrenaline) ready; train staff in basic life support.

## 3.3 Vaccination failure

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Vaccine failure** | Occurrence of the specific vaccine-preventable disease in a person who was appropriately and fully vaccinated |
| **Primary failure** | Person never develops protective immunity after vaccination (no seroconversion) |
| **Secondary failure** | Immunity develops at first but wanes over time |
| **Failure due to vaccination (programme) problems** | Vaccine not given correctly: cold-chain break, expired vaccine, wrong dose schedule, wrong route |
| **Failure due to vaccinee** | Immunodeficiency, immunosuppressive drugs, interfering maternal antibodies, concurrent infection |
| **Failure due to vaccine** | Strain not covered by the vaccine, inherent lower efficacy, poor-quality lot |

Confirmed failure needs laboratory proof of disease (and ideally of the pathogen strain); suspected failure is based on clinical diagnosis. Failure reports are part of vaccine pharmacovigilance because they may reveal quality or cold-chain problems.

## 3.4 Pharmacovigilance methods — overview

```text
                     PHARMACOVIGILANCE METHODS
  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
Passive surveillance   Active surveillance   Comparative        Targeted clinical
 - spontaneous reports  - sentinel sites       observational      investigations
 - case series          - drug event           studies            (studies in
Stimulated reporting      monitoring           - cross-sectional   specific groups,
                        - registries           - case-control      PK, interactions)
                                               - cohort
```

## 3.5 Passive surveillance

**Spontaneous reporting** — health professionals (and patients) voluntarily report suspected ADRs to a national centre or the MAH on a standard form. Examples: PvPI form, UK Yellow Card, US MedWatch.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Cheap and simple; covers all drugs and all patients | **Under-reporting** (often most ADRs are never reported) |
| Works for the whole life of a drug | Reporting bias: new drugs, serious and media-publicised reactions over-reported |
| Best method to find **rare, new, unexpected** reactions — the main source of signals | No denominator — cannot calculate incidence |
| Generates hypotheses quickly | Poor quality or incomplete reports; duplicates |
| Includes special groups excluded from trials | Cannot easily detect delayed or common-background events |

**Case series** — a collection of reports of the same reaction with the same drug. A well-documented case series (for example, the thalidomide reports) can establish a signal, especially for rare events with almost no background rate. It cannot give rates or prove causation alone.

## 3.6 Stimulated reporting

Methods that **encourage and make easier** the reporting of particular events or drugs for a period:

- reporting campaigns, posters, CMEs and online reporting for new drugs;
- **black triangle**-type schemes that ask for all reactions to new medicines to be reported;
- **early post-marketing phase vigilance** (used in Japan) — intensive reporting during the first six months after launch;
- focused programmes in public health campaigns (for example, new antimalarials or antiretrovirals).

Stimulated reports are still spontaneous reports and must be interpreted carefully because the stimulation itself changes reporting rates.

## 3.7 Active surveillance

Active surveillance tries to find **all** events in a defined population through an organised process, giving more complete data and often a denominator.

**a) Sentinel sites** — selected hospitals or clinics where staff actively review records, interview patients and capture all events in patients on a drug. Good for high-risk groups and drugs used in hospital.

**b) Drug event monitoring (prescription event monitoring, PEM)**

1. Patients are identified from prescriptions (in the UK, through the Drug Safety Research Unit).
2. Questionnaires are sent to the prescribing doctors after a set time asking about **any event**, not just suspected ADRs.
3. Event rates are calculated for the cohort (often around 10,000 patients) and compared over time or with other drugs.

The **cohort event monitoring** used by WHO in public health programmes (for example, antimalarials and antiretrovirals) works on the same principle.

**c) Registries** — lists of patients with the same exposure (**drug registry**, for example a pregnancy exposure registry) or the same disease/outcome (**disease registry**, for example a registry of aplastic anaemia or birth defects). Used to compare outcomes in exposed and unexposed people.

**d) Automated database / record linkage** — electronic health records and insurance claims databases searched for exposure and outcome.

## 3.8 Comparative observational studies (pharmacoepidemiology)

**Pharmacoepidemiology** is the study of the use and effects of drugs in large numbers of people. It applies epidemiological methods to clinical pharmacology.

**a) Cross-sectional study** — data on exposure and outcome collected at one point in time (a survey or snapshot).

- Measures **prevalence** of drug use or ADRs; quick and cheap.
- Cannot establish whether exposure came before the outcome, so it is weak for causation.
- Example: a survey of prevalence of ADRs among patients admitted to a hospital on one day.

**b) Case-control study** — start from the **outcome**.

```text
           Exposed to drug?    Yes   No
Cases (with ADR/disease)         a     b
Controls (without)               c     d

Odds ratio (OR) = (a × d) / (b × c)
```

- Compares past drug exposure in **cases** with that in **controls**.
- Efficient for **rare outcomes** and long latency; fewer patients, cheaper.
- Weaknesses: recall bias, selection bias, cannot give incidence directly.
- Classic examples: diethylstilbestrol in pregnancy and vaginal clear-cell adenocarcinoma in daughters; aspirin and Reye's syndrome in children.

**c) Cohort study** — start from **exposure** and follow people forward.

```text
                     Developed ADR?    Yes    No
Exposed to drug                          a      b
Not exposed                              c      d

Relative risk (RR) = [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]
Attributable (excess) risk = a/(a+b) − c/(c+d)
```

- Prospective (follow from now) or retrospective (historical records).
- Gives **incidence**, relative risk, and can study several outcomes of one exposure.
- Weaknesses: large and long for rare events, costly, loss to follow-up, confounding.
- Example: oral contraceptives and venous thromboembolism.

**Comparison**

| Feature | Cross-sectional | Case-control | Cohort |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starting point | Population at one time | Outcome | Exposure |
| Direction | Snapshot | Backward | Forward (or historical) |
| Measure | Prevalence | Odds ratio | Incidence, relative risk |
| Best for | Burden of drug use or ADRs | Rare outcomes | Rare exposures, several outcomes |
| Main bias | Temporality unclear | Recall and selection | Loss to follow-up |

**Confounding** — a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome (for example, "confounding by indication": sicker patients get a particular drug). Controlled by matching, restriction, stratification and statistical adjustment.

## 3.9 Targeted clinical investigations

When a signal is found, specific studies may be designed to test it:

- **pharmacokinetic studies** in groups at risk (elderly, renal or hepatic impairment);
- **drug interaction studies**;
- **pharmacogenetic studies** to find genetic risk factors;
- laboratory or mechanistic studies;
- **large simple trials** — randomised studies with minimal data collection in many patients, to compare risks of rare outcomes between treatments.

## 3.10 Signal detection

**Signal (WHO)** — reported information on a possible causal relationship between an adverse event and a drug, the relationship being unknown or incompletely documented previously. Usually more than one report is needed.

**Qualitative detection** — clinical review of individual reports and case series: unusual or serious events, positive rechallenge, designated medical events (for example, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, agranulocytosis, liver failure).

**Quantitative detection (disproportionality analysis)** — compares how often an event is reported with a drug against how often it is reported with all other drugs in the database.

```text
                     Event of interest    All other events
Drug of interest            a                  b
All other drugs             c                  d

Proportional reporting ratio  PRR = [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]
Reporting odds ratio          ROR = (a × d) / (b × c)
```

- A common screening rule: **PRR ≥ 2, chi-square ≥ 4 and at least 3 cases**.
- **Information component (IC)** — Bayesian measure used by WHO–UMC (Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network); a signal is flagged when the lower limit of its credibility interval is above zero.
- **Empirical Bayes geometric mean (EBGM)** — used by the US FDA (multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker).

Disproportionality shows a **statistical association in reporting**, not proof of risk; every statistical signal needs clinical review.

**Signal management process**

1. Signal detection
2. Signal validation (is there enough evidence to look further?)
3. Analysis and prioritisation (seriousness, public health impact)
4. Signal assessment (all data: trials, literature, mechanism, studies)
5. Recommendation for action (label change, restriction, study, withdrawal)
6. Exchange of information with regulators and partners

## 3.11 Communication in pharmacovigilance

**Effective communication** means giving the right safety information to the right people at the right time in a form they can understand and act on.

**Principles** (reflected in the WHO-supported **Erice Declaration, 1997** on communicating drug safety information):

- Information should be honest, evidence-based, transparent and timely.
- Uncertainty should be explained, not hidden.
- Benefits must be presented alongside risks.
- Patients and the public have a right to safety information.
- Education in understanding and using safety information is needed for professionals and the public.

**Tools:** label changes (contraindications, warnings, boxed warnings), Dear Healthcare Professional letters (DHPC), drug safety alerts and newsletters (for example, PvPI alerts), patient information leaflets, medication guides, websites and press releases, educational material under risk-minimisation plans.

## 3.12 Communication in a drug safety crisis

A **drug safety crisis** is a sudden situation (serious new ADR, contamination, media report, deaths) that threatens patients and public confidence and needs urgent decisions.

**Crisis management steps**

1. **Preparation** — a crisis management plan, a named team (safety, medical, regulatory, legal, quality, communications), a single trained spokesperson, contact lists.
2. **Rapid assessment** — collect and verify facts, assess the scale and risk.
3. **Decision** — protective action (batch recall, suspension, restriction, label change) in agreement with the regulator.
4. **Communication** — fast, consistent, honest messages to each audience.
5. **Follow-up** — monitor the situation, correct misinformation, review lessons learned.

**Communicating with different audiences**

| Audience | How and what |
| --- | --- |
| Regulatory agencies | Immediate notification, expedited reports, joint decisions on action; honest disclosure of all data |
| Business partners | Safety data exchange agreements; prompt sharing of cases and decisions with licensors, distributors, CROs |
| Healthcare facilities and professionals | DHPC letters, alerts, revised guidance, advice on managing patients already exposed |
| Media and public | Press releases and briefings through one spokesperson; plain language; explain risk in context with benefits; avoid speculation |
| Patients | What to do: do not stop essential drugs without advice; where to report problems |

## Remember

- AEFI does not need a causal link; 5 cause types: vaccine product, quality defect, immunisation error, immunisation anxiety, coincidental.
- WHO AEFI causality: consistent, indeterminate, inconsistent, unclassifiable. Brighton Collaboration gives case definitions.
- Vaccine failure: primary (never immune) vs secondary (waning).
- Passive = spontaneous reports (cheap, best for rare new ADRs, under-reporting, no denominator).
- Active = sentinel sites, PEM/cohort event monitoring, registries.
- Case-control → odds ratio (rare outcomes); cohort → relative risk and incidence; cross-sectional → prevalence.
- PRR = [a/(a+b)]/[c/(c+d)]; ROR = ad/bc; WHO–UMC uses IC; FDA uses EBGM.
- Crisis: one spokesperson, fast, honest, audience-specific messages; Erice Declaration 1997.

# Unit 4: Safety data generation and ICH guidelines for pharmacovigilance

Safety information about a medicine is built up in layers: animal studies before it is given to humans, carefully watched clinical trials, and then years of real-world use. Each stage has its own rules for collecting and reporting safety data, and the most widely used rules are the E2 guidelines of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH). This unit follows a drug from the laboratory to the market and then covers expedited reporting, individual case safety reports, periodic safety update reports, post-approval reporting, pharmacovigilance planning and good clinical practice in safety studies.

## 4.1 Safety data generation — the life cycle

```text
Pre-clinical (animal, in vitro)  →  Phase I  →  Phase II  →  Phase III  →  Approval  →  Phase IV / PMS
   toxicity profile, safe          first in    efficacy in   large trials,              real-world use,
   starting dose                   humans,     patients,     common ADRs                rare, delayed and
                                   tolerability dose range                              special-group ADRs
```

## 4.2 Pre-clinical phase

Pre-clinical safety studies identify target organs of toxicity, reversibility, a safe starting point for human trials and parameters to monitor in patients. They follow Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) and the ICH safety (S) guidelines; animal use in India is controlled by the CCSEA (formerly CPCSEA).

| Study | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Single-dose (acute) toxicity | Effects after one administration; signs and target organs |
| Repeated-dose toxicity (sub-acute, sub-chronic, chronic) | Effects of continued use; duration linked to planned clinical use |
| Safety pharmacology | Effects on vital functions — CNS, cardiovascular (including QT prolongation, hERG testing) and respiratory systems (ICH S7A, S7B) |
| Genotoxicity | Gene mutation (Ames test), chromosomal damage (in vitro and in vivo micronucleus) |
| Carcinogenicity | Lifetime studies for drugs used long term or with concern |
| Reproductive and developmental toxicity | Fertility, embryo-fetal development (teratogenicity), pre- and post-natal development |
| Toxicokinetics | Exposure in the toxicity studies, linking findings to blood levels |
| Local tolerance, immunotoxicity, phototoxicity, dependence | As needed for route and class |

**Limits:** species differences (thalidomide's teratogenicity was not seen in the rodent tests used at the time), high doses, idiosyncratic reactions are not predictable in animals.

## 4.3 Clinical phase

| Phase | Subjects | Safety focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Small number of healthy volunteers (or patients for cytotoxic drugs) | Tolerability, pharmacokinetics, dose-limiting effects |
| II | Some hundreds of patients | Short-term safety, dose–response, common ADRs |
| III | Several hundreds to thousands of patients, often randomised controlled | Common and less common ADRs, comparison with standard treatment, benefit–risk for approval |

**Safety tools during trials**

- **Investigator's Brochure (IB)** — contains the **reference safety information** used to decide whether a reaction is "expected".
- **Adverse event collection** at every visit; **serious adverse events (SAEs)** reported by the investigator to the sponsor quickly.
- **SUSARs** (suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions) reported to regulators on an expedited basis.
- **Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB)** — independent experts who review unblinded safety data and can recommend stopping a trial.
- **Development Safety Update Report (DSUR, ICH E2F)** — annual review of the safety of a drug under development.

## 4.4 Post-approval phase — post-marketing surveillance (PMS)

**PMS** is the monitoring of a medicine after it is marketed, to find ADRs not seen in trials and to confirm the benefit–risk balance in real use.

**Methods:** spontaneous reports, solicited reports from patient support programmes, literature monitoring, **post-authorisation safety studies (PASS)**, phase IV trials, registries, drug utilisation studies, periodic reports (PSUR/PBRER), risk management plans.

**Possible outcomes:** new warnings or contraindications, dose changes, restricted use or prescriber, additional monitoring, boxed warning, suspension or withdrawal (for example, rofecoxib, cerivastatin).

## 4.5 ICH — organisation and objectives

The **International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH)** was founded in **1990** by the regulators and industry associations of the **European Union, Japan and the United States**. In **2015** it was reorganised as an international non-profit association under Swiss law and took its present name (earlier it was the International *Conference* on Harmonisation). Many other regulators have since joined as members or observers.

**Founding parties**

| Region | Regulator | Industry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU | European Commission / EMA | EFPIA |
| Japan | MHLW / PMDA | JPMA |
| USA | FDA | PhRMA |

**Structure:** Assembly (decision-making body of all members), Management Committee, MedDRA Management Committee, Secretariat in Geneva, and expert working groups that draft guidelines.

**Objectives**

1. Harmonise technical requirements for registering medicines.
2. Avoid duplication of animal and human testing.
3. Make development faster and cheaper without lowering quality, safety or efficacy.
4. Enable better use of resources and faster access of patients to new medicines.
5. Provide common standards for electronic exchange of data (MedDRA, E2B, eCTD).

**Guideline categories:** **Q** (quality), **S** (safety — non-clinical), **E** (efficacy — clinical, including the pharmacovigilance E2 series and GCP E6), **M** (multidisciplinary — MedDRA, CTD).

**ICH process steps:** 1 consensus building → 2 draft agreed for consultation → 3 regulatory consultation and revision → 4 adoption of the final harmonised guideline → 5 implementation in each region.

**The E2 (pharmacovigilance) series**

| Guideline | Topic |
| --- | --- |
| E2A (1994) | Clinical safety data management: definitions and standards for expedited reporting |
| E2B | Data elements for electronic transmission of individual case safety reports (current version E2B(R3)) |
| E2C | Periodic safety update reports; revised as E2C(R2) **Periodic Benefit–Risk Evaluation Report (PBRER)** in 2012 |
| E2D | Post-approval safety data management (2003; revised as E2D(R1) in 2025) |
| E2E (2004) | Pharmacovigilance planning |
| E2F (2010) | Development Safety Update Report (DSUR) |

## 4.6 Expedited reporting (ICH E2A)

**Key definitions (E2A):** adverse event, adverse drug reaction (in clinical trials, a noxious and unintended response to a medicinal product related to any dose, where a causal relationship is at least a reasonable possibility), **unexpected** ADR (not consistent with the IB or label), **serious** (death, life-threatening, hospitalisation or prolongation, persistent or significant disability, congenital anomaly, medically important).

**What must be expedited:** all suspected ADRs that are **both serious and unexpected**.

| Type of case | Timeline (from day 0 = first receipt of the minimum information) |
| --- | --- |
| Fatal or life-threatening, unexpected ADR | As soon as possible, **no later than 7 calendar days**; a complete follow-up report within **8 more days** |
| Other serious, unexpected ADR | As soon as possible, **no later than 15 calendar days** |
| Other information that changes the benefit–risk (e.g. a significant increase in rate of an expected serious ADR, a finding in animal studies) | Also expedited, usually within 15 days |

**Not usually expedited:** non-serious ADRs, serious **expected** ADRs (summarised in periodic reports), events judged not related.

**Other E2A points**

- Blinded cases: the blind is usually broken for the individual SUSAR before reporting.
- Reports should use a standard format (CIOMS I form or electronic E2B).
- Minimum information: identifiable patient, identifiable reporter, suspect product, reaction.

## 4.7 Individual case safety reports (ICSR) — ICH E2B

An **ICSR** is the format and content for reporting one or more suspected adverse reactions in **one patient** at a specific time.

**E2B** defines the standard **data elements** so that reports can be sent electronically between companies, regulators and the WHO. E2B(R3) uses the HL7 ICSR XML message format.

**Main sections of an ICSR**

1. Case administrative information — unique case identifier, dates of receipt, type of report (spontaneous, study, literature), seriousness criteria.
2. Primary source (reporter) — qualification, country.
3. Sender and receiver information.
4. Literature reference and study identification (if any).
5. Patient characteristics — initials, age, sex, weight, medical history, past drug history, death details.
6. Reaction/event — verbatim and MedDRA terms, onset, outcome.
7. Results of tests and procedures.
8. Drug information — suspect, concomitant and interacting drugs; dose, route, dates, indication, action taken, dechallenge/rechallenge.
9. Narrative case summary, reporter's and sender's comments, causality.

**Validity:** a case is valid only with the four minimum criteria. Missing details are sought by **follow-up**; each follow-up is sent as a new version of the same case.

## 4.8 Writing case narratives

A **case narrative** is a clear, complete, chronological story of the case that can be understood without the rest of the report.

**Structure**

1. Opening: report source and type; patient age, sex (and relevant weight).
2. Relevant medical history, risk factors, allergies.
3. Concomitant medicines.
4. Suspect drug: indication, dose, route, start date.
5. The event: onset (time from first dose), signs and symptoms, diagnosis.
6. Relevant investigations with values, units and dates.
7. Treatment of the event.
8. Action taken with the drug; dechallenge and rechallenge results.
9. Outcome and date (recovered, recovering, not recovered, recovered with sequelae, fatal, unknown).
10. Reporter's assessment of seriousness and causality; sender's comment.

**Qualities of a good narrative:** accurate (matches the data fields), complete, objective (no blame or speculation), chronological, concise, no unexplained abbreviations, protects identity (initials only), consistent with MedDRA coding.

## 4.9 Periodic safety update reports (PSUR) — ICH E2C

A **PSUR** is a periodic report from the MAH that presents worldwide safety experience of a medicine over a defined period after approval, with an evaluation of whether the benefit–risk balance has changed.

**Key concepts**

- **International Birth Date (IBD)** — the date of the first marketing approval anywhere in the world; reporting periods are aligned to it.
- **Data lock point (DLP)** — the cut-off date for data included in a report.
- **Reference safety information** — the company core safety information against which expectedness is judged.

**Classical PSUR contents**

1. Introduction
2. Worldwide marketing authorisation status
3. Actions taken for safety reasons in the period
4. Changes to reference safety information
5. Patient exposure
6. Individual case histories (line listings and summary tabulations)
7. Studies (new, ongoing, published)
8. Other information (efficacy, late-breaking data)
9. Overall safety evaluation
10. Conclusion

**PBRER — E2C(R2), 2012.** The PSUR was converted into the **Periodic Benefit–Risk Evaluation Report**, which:

- evaluates **benefits as well as risks** and gives an integrated benefit–risk analysis;
- considers **cumulative** data, not just the interval;
- has sections on signals (new, ongoing, closed), signal and risk evaluation, benefit evaluation and integrated benefit–risk analysis;
- is modular, so sections can be reused in the DSUR and RMP.

**Frequency:** set by each regulator; in India the rules require PSURs every six months for the first two years after approval and annually for the next two years (see Unit 5).

## 4.10 Post-approval expedited reporting — ICH E2D

**Sources of post-approval reports**

| Unsolicited | Solicited |
| --- | --- |
| Spontaneous reports from professionals and consumers | Reports from organised data collection: patient support programmes, surveys, registries, post-approval studies |
| Literature reports | Treated like study reports — need a causality assessment |
| Internet and digital media, other sources | |

**Rules**

- Spontaneous reports are considered to carry an **implied suspicion** of causality.
- **Serious, unexpected** ADRs from any source are expedited **within 15 calendar days**.
- Literature must be screened regularly; the date the MAH becomes aware of a published case is day 0.
- Special situations to be collected: lack of efficacy, overdose, abuse, misuse, medication errors, exposure during pregnancy and breastfeeding, occupational exposure.
- Good case management practices: follow-up, duplicate detection, data quality.

## 4.11 Pharmacovigilance planning — ICH E2E

E2E describes how to plan PV activities, especially around the time of approval, for new drugs or new indications.

**Two parts**

1. **Safety specification** — summary of what is known and not known:
   - **important identified risks** (proven by adequate evidence);
   - **important potential risks** (suspected, not confirmed);
   - **missing information** (populations not studied — children, pregnancy, hepatic impairment).
2. **Pharmacovigilance plan** — how each issue will be addressed:
   - **routine pharmacovigilance** (spontaneous reporting, PSURs, signal detection) for all products;
   - **additional activities** (PASS, registries, active surveillance, targeted studies) for specific concerns, with milestones.

E2E is the basis of the **Risk Management Plan (RMP)**, which adds **risk minimisation measures** — routine (labelling, pack size, legal status) and additional (educational material, controlled access, pregnancy prevention programmes).

## 4.12 Good clinical practice in pharmacovigilance studies

**GCP (ICH E6)** is the international ethical and scientific quality standard for designing, conducting, recording and reporting trials with human subjects. The current version is E6(R3), adopted by ICH in 2025.

**Core principles applied to safety studies**

1. Rights, safety and well-being of participants come first (Declaration of Helsinki).
2. Approval by an **ethics committee** and **informed consent** before participation.
3. A scientifically sound **protocol**, followed carefully.
4. Qualified investigators and trained staff.
5. Accurate, verifiable, protected data (data integrity, confidentiality).
6. Prompt recording and reporting of **adverse events and SAEs** by the investigator to the sponsor, and of SUSARs by the sponsor to regulators and ethics committees.
7. Monitoring, audits and quality management by the sponsor.

**Non-interventional (observational) safety studies** are not trials, but similar principles apply through **Good Pharmacoepidemiology Practice** and regulatory guidance on PASS: a written protocol, ethics review where needed, data protection, reporting of adverse reactions found during the study, and publication of results.

## Remember

- Pre-clinical → phases I–III → approval → phase IV/PMS; trials are too small to see rare ADRs.
- ICH founded **1990** (EU, Japan, USA; regulators + industry); renamed **Council** in **2015**; guidelines Q, S, E, M.
- E2A definitions and expedited reporting; E2B ICSR data elements; E2C PSUR → PBRER (R2, 2012); E2D post-approval; E2E PV planning; E2F DSUR; E6 GCP.
- Expedited: serious + unexpected. Fatal/life-threatening **7 days** (+8 for follow-up); other serious unexpected **15 days**.
- Minimum valid case: patient, reporter, suspect drug, reaction.
- PSUR keys: IBD, data lock point, reference safety information.
- E2E: safety specification (identified risks, potential risks, missing information) + PV plan (routine + additional) → RMP.

# Unit 5: Pharmacogenomics of ADRs, special populations, CIOMS and CDSCO

The same medicine at the same dose can be harmless in one person and dangerous in another. Genes, age, pregnancy and breastfeeding change how a drug is handled and how the body responds. This unit explains the genetic basis of many ADRs (with a focus on pharmacokinetic genes), how drug safety is judged in children, pregnant and breastfeeding women and the elderly, the international CIOMS standards for ADR reporting, and the Indian regulatory framework — CDSCO, the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Schedule Y — compared with global requirements.

## 5.1 Pharmacogenomics of adverse drug reactions

**Pharmacogenetics** — study of how inherited differences in single genes change drug response. **Pharmacogenomics** — the genome-wide study of these differences. Both explain many type B ("idiosyncratic") reactions and some type A reactions that occur at normal doses.

**Genetic polymorphism** — a variant of a gene present in more than 1% of a population. Depending on their genes, people are grouped as **poor, intermediate, normal (extensive) or ultrarapid metabolisers**.

```text
Poor metaboliser        →  drug accumulates  → type A toxicity at normal doses
                           (prodrug: no active form → therapeutic failure)
Ultrarapid metaboliser  →  drug cleared fast → failure
                           (prodrug: too much active form → toxicity)
```

## 5.2 Genetics-related ADRs affecting pharmacokinetics

| Gene / enzyme | Effect of variant | Drugs | ADR / consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **CYP2D6** | Poor and ultrarapid metabolisers | Codeine and tramadol (prodrugs activated by CYP2D6) | Ultrarapid: excess morphine → respiratory depression (deaths reported in children and breastfed infants); poor: no analgesia |
| CYP2D6 | Poor metabolisers | Some tricyclic antidepressants, metoprolol | Higher levels → anticholinergic, cardiac effects; bradycardia |
| **CYP2C9** (with VKORC1, a pharmacodynamic gene) | Reduced activity | Warfarin, phenytoin | Over-anticoagulation and bleeding; phenytoin toxicity |
| **CYP2C19** | Poor metabolisers | Clopidogrel (prodrug) | Less active metabolite → reduced antiplatelet effect, stent thrombosis |
| CYP2C19 | Poor metabolisers | Proton pump inhibitors | Higher exposure (greater acid suppression) |
| **N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2)** | **Slow acetylators** | Isoniazid | Peripheral neuropathy, hepatotoxicity |
| NAT2 slow acetylators | | Hydralazine, procainamide | Drug-induced lupus |
| **TPMT** (thiopurine methyltransferase), also NUDT15 | Low activity | Azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine | Severe bone-marrow suppression |
| **DPYD** (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase) | Deficiency | 5-fluorouracil, capecitabine | Severe mucositis, neutropenia, diarrhoea, can be fatal |
| **UGT1A1*28** (Gilbert-type variant) | Reduced glucuronidation | Irinotecan | Neutropenia and diarrhoea |
| **Plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase** (BCHE) | Atypical enzyme | Succinylcholine (suxamethonium), mivacurium | Prolonged apnoea after anaesthesia |
| **G6PD** deficiency (red-cell enzyme) | Low NADPH in red cells | Primaquine, dapsone, sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase | Acute haemolytic anaemia |

**Pharmacodynamic and immune examples (HLA)**

| HLA allele | Drug | Reaction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HLA-B\*57:01 | Abacavir | Hypersensitivity syndrome (screening before use is standard) |
| HLA-B\*15:02 | Carbamazepine (and phenytoin) | Stevens–Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis, mainly in South-East and South Asian populations |
| HLA-B\*58:01 | Allopurinol | SJS/TEN, DRESS |
| — | Halothane, succinylcholine (RYR1 variants) | Malignant hyperthermia |

**Applications in pharmacovigilance**

- Explains clusters of ADRs in certain ethnic groups (CYP2C19 poor metabolisers and HLA-B\*15:02 are more common in Asian populations).
- Pre-treatment **genetic testing** (HLA-B\*57:01, TPMT, DPYD) prevents serious reactions.
- **Genotype-guided dosing** (warfarin with CYP2C9/VKORC1).
- Labels now include pharmacogenomic information (boxed warnings, testing recommendations).
- Collection of DNA samples in case-control studies of serious ADRs (SJS/TEN, liver injury).

## 5.3 Drug safety evaluation in paediatrics

**Why children are special**

- Children are **under-represented in trials**; much paediatric prescribing is **off-label** or unlicensed.
- Age-related changes in pharmacokinetics:

| PK step | Neonates and infants compared with adults |
| --- | --- |
| Absorption | Higher gastric pH, irregular emptying; thinner skin with greater topical absorption |
| Distribution | More body water, less fat; lower plasma protein binding; more permeable blood–brain barrier |
| Metabolism | Immature enzymes, especially glucuronidation, at birth; faster than adults in older children |
| Excretion | Lower glomerular filtration and tubular secretion in neonates |

- Weight-based and body-surface dosing; risk of calculation errors (tenfold errors), lack of child-friendly dosage forms.
- Effects on **growth and development** may appear years later.

**Classic paediatric ADRs**

| Drug | ADR |
| --- | --- |
| Chloramphenicol in neonates | Grey baby syndrome (immature glucuronidation) |
| Sulphonamides, ceftriaxone in neonates | Kernicterus from displacement of bilirubin |
| Tetracyclines | Discoloration of teeth, effect on bone growth |
| Fluoroquinolones | Concern over cartilage damage (seen in young animals) |
| Aspirin | Reye's syndrome in children with viral illness |
| Benzyl alcohol preservative | Gasping syndrome in neonates |
| Codeine | Respiratory depression in ultrarapid metabolisers |

**PV measures:** paediatric investigation plans and age-appropriate trials, paediatric formulations, active surveillance in neonatal and paediatric units, paediatric-specific reporting, causality assessment with age-specific background rates, and careful counselling of parents.

## 5.4 Drug safety in pregnancy

**Why it is difficult:** pregnant women are excluded from almost all trials, so human data come mainly from post-marketing reports, registries and observational studies. Two lives are exposed; effects may be delayed (as with diethylstilbestrol).

**Physiological changes:** increased plasma volume and body water, reduced albumin, increased glomerular filtration, altered hepatic enzyme activity — so drug levels may change.

**Timing of exposure**

```text
Weeks after conception:  0–2            3–8                 9 to term
                         "all or none"  ORGANOGENESIS       growth and functional
                         (loss or no    (major structural   development (growth
                         effect)        malformations)      restriction, organ toxicity)
```

**Known teratogens and fetotoxic drugs (examples)**

| Drug | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Thalidomide | Phocomelia (limb defects) |
| Isotretinoin and other retinoids | Severe craniofacial, cardiac and CNS defects |
| Sodium valproate | Neural tube defects; developmental problems |
| Warfarin | Fetal warfarin syndrome (nasal hypoplasia, bone stippling); bleeding |
| Phenytoin | Fetal hydantoin syndrome |
| ACE inhibitors, ARBs (2nd and 3rd trimester) | Fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios |
| Tetracyclines | Teeth and bone effects |
| Diethylstilbestrol | Vaginal clear-cell adenocarcinoma in daughters |
| Methotrexate | Abortion, malformations |

**Risk classification.** The older US FDA letter categories (A, B, C, D, X) were replaced in 2015 by the **Pregnancy and Lactation Labelling Rule**, which uses narrative sections (risk summary, clinical considerations, data) instead of letters. Many Indian textbooks still describe the letter categories, so know both.

**PV methods in pregnancy:** pregnancy exposure registries, follow-up of every exposed pregnancy reported (collect outcome at birth and later), birth-defect registries, case-control studies of malformations, teratology information services, and linkage of mother and child records. Exposure during pregnancy is reported even without an adverse outcome.

## 5.5 Drug safety in lactation

**Transfer into milk depends on:**

- **lipid solubility** (high → more transfer);
- **molecular weight** (small molecules pass easily);
- **protein binding** (highly bound drugs pass less);
- **ionisation** — milk is slightly more acidic than plasma, so **weak bases** are trapped in milk;
- maternal plasma level, half-life, timing of feeds;
- oral bioavailability in the infant and infant's age (premature babies at greater risk).

**Measures:** milk-to-plasma (M/P) ratio; **relative infant dose** (infant dose via milk as a percentage of the mother's weight-adjusted dose — values under about 10% are generally considered compatible).

**Drugs needing caution or avoidance (examples):** anticancer drugs, radioactive agents, lithium, amiodarone, ergot alkaloids (suppress lactation), and codeine (infant respiratory depression when the mother is an ultrarapid metaboliser).

**PV in lactation:** report infant effects (sedation, poor feeding, rash), use resources such as LactMed, prefer drugs with established safety, time doses just after feeds.

## 5.6 Drug safety in geriatrics

**Why the elderly are at higher risk**

- **Polypharmacy** — many diseases, many prescribers, more interactions.
- **Pharmacokinetic changes:** reduced renal function (most important), reduced liver blood flow and mass, more body fat and less body water (fat-soluble drugs last longer, water-soluble drugs reach higher levels), lower albumin.
- **Pharmacodynamic changes:** increased sensitivity to CNS-acting drugs, blunted baroreceptor reflexes (postural hypotension), impaired homeostasis.
- Cognitive impairment, poor vision, swallowing problems → adherence errors.
- **Prescribing cascade** — an ADR mistaken for a new disease and treated with another drug.
- Under-represented in trials, especially the very old and frail.

**Common geriatric ADRs**

| Drug group | ADR |
| --- | --- |
| Benzodiazepines, sedatives, antipsychotics | Falls, fractures, confusion |
| Anticholinergics (first-generation antihistamines, tricyclics) | Confusion, urinary retention, constipation |
| NSAIDs | GI bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention |
| Diuretics, SSRIs | Hyponatraemia |
| Digoxin | Toxicity (renal decline) |
| Antihypertensives | Postural hypotension, falls |
| Anticoagulants | Bleeding |

**Tools:** **Beers criteria** (American Geriatrics Society list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults), **STOPP/START** criteria (screening for inappropriate prescriptions and omitted beneficial ones), medication review by pharmacists, renal dose adjustment, deprescribing.

## 5.7 CIOMS

The **Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS)** is an international non-governmental organisation set up in **1949 by WHO and UNESCO**, based in Geneva. Its working groups bring together regulators, industry and academics to propose harmonised approaches; many CIOMS proposals later became ICH guidelines.

**Important CIOMS working groups**

| Group | Topic and outcome |
| --- | --- |
| CIOMS I | International reporting of individual ADRs — the **CIOMS I form**; basis of ICH E2A |
| CIOMS II | Periodic safety update summaries — basis of the PSUR (ICH E2C) |
| CIOMS III | Core clinical safety information (company core data sheet) |
| CIOMS IV | Benefit–risk balance for marketed drugs |
| CIOMS V | Current challenges: consumer reports, literature, solicited reports, lack of efficacy |
| CIOMS VI | Management of safety information from clinical trials |
| CIOMS VII | Development safety update report (basis of ICH E2F) |
| CIOMS VIII | Practical aspects of signal detection |
| CIOMS IX | Risk minimisation |
| CIOMS X | Meta-analysis in safety evaluation |

CIOMS also publishes **international ethical guidelines for health-related research** and the frequency terms (very common to very rare) used in labelling.

**CIOMS I form** — the standard paper form for reporting a single suspected ADR from manufacturers to regulators. Sections:

1. **Reaction information** — patient initials, country, date of birth/age, sex, reaction onset date, description of the reaction including relevant tests, seriousness tick-boxes (patient died, involved or prolonged hospitalisation, persistent disability or incapacity, life-threatening).
2. **Suspect drug information** — drug name, daily dose, route, indication, therapy dates and duration; did the reaction abate after stopping? did it reappear after reintroduction?
3. **Concomitant drugs and history** — other drugs with dates, relevant history (diagnoses, allergies, pregnancy).
4. **Manufacturer information** — name and address, manufacturer control number, date received, report source (study, literature, health professional), report type (initial or follow-up).

## 5.8 CDSCO (India) and pharmacovigilance

The **Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO)**, under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, is India's national drug regulator, headed by the **Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI)**.

**PV-related functions**

- Approval of new drugs and clinical trials; conditions for post-marketing studies.
- Receiving SAE reports from trials, PSURs and serious ADR reports from MAHs.
- Acting on PvPI recommendations: label changes, safety alerts, restrictions, suspension or prohibition of drugs and irrational fixed-dose combinations.
- Inspections and enforcement under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
- Working with IPC (PvPI), the Materiovigilance programme and state drug controllers.
- With IPC it has issued pharmacovigilance guidance for marketing authorisation holders (first version 2018), requiring companies to have a PV system, a person responsible for PV, and timely reporting of ADRs to the national programme.

## 5.9 Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Schedule Y

- **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** and **Rules, 1945** — the main law on import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs in India.
- **Schedule Y** of the Rules (major revision in **2005**) set requirements for permission to import or manufacture new drugs and to conduct clinical trials. PV-related points:
  - **PSURs** for a new drug: every **six months for the first two years** after approval, then **annually for the next two years**.
  - Reporting of **serious adverse events** in clinical trials by the investigator to the sponsor, ethics committee and licensing authority within short fixed timelines, followed by an analysed report.
  - Formats for SAE reporting and for clinical study reports; requirements for informed consent and ethics committees.
- In **2019** the clinical trial and new drug provisions of Schedule Y were replaced by the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**, which keep the six-monthly then annual PSUR requirement and set fixed timelines: the investigator reports an SAE **within 24 hours**, and an analysed report follows **within 14 days**. Questions set on the PCI syllabus still use the term Schedule Y, so describe both.

## 5.10 Differences between Indian and global pharmacovigilance requirements

| Aspect | India | Global (ICH regions, EU, USA) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National system | PvPI under IPC with AMCs mostly in medical colleges; CDSCO as regulator | Long-established systems: EU EudraVigilance, US FAERS, UK Yellow Card |
| Legal basis | D&C Act and Rules, NDCT Rules 2019, PvPI guidance for MAHs | Detailed laws and guidance (EU Good Pharmacovigilance Practices modules, US federal regulations) |
| Responsible person | Person responsible for PV in the company, as per guidance | EU: Qualified Person for PV (QPPV) resident in the EU, PV System Master File |
| Periodic reports | PSUR 6-monthly × 2 years, then annual × 2 years | PBRER with EU reference dates; frequency set by risk |
| Risk management | Less formal RMP requirements | RMP mandatory in EU; REMS in USA |
| Signal management | Mainly at NCC level | Formal signal management by MAHs and regulators |
| Reporting culture | Under-reporting; low awareness among doctors and pharmacists; growing consumer reporting | Higher reporting rates, mature consumer reporting |
| Special issues | Many brands and FDCs, self-medication, OTC misuse, traditional medicines (AYUSH has a separate PV scheme), language diversity, substandard drugs | Biosimilar tracking, large electronic health record networks for active surveillance |

**Common ground:** ICH definitions (E2A), MedDRA coding, E2B electronic reporting through VigiFlow, WHO programme membership.

## Remember

- Polymorphism → poor / intermediate / normal / ultrarapid metabolisers.
- CYP2D6 codeine, CYP2C9 warfarin, CYP2C19 clopidogrel, NAT2 isoniazid (slow acetylators), TPMT azathioprine, DPYD 5-FU, UGT1A1 irinotecan, pseudocholinesterase succinylcholine, G6PD primaquine; HLA-B\*15:02 carbamazepine, HLA-B\*57:01 abacavir, HLA-B\*58:01 allopurinol.
- Children: grey baby, kernicterus, teeth staining, Reye's syndrome.
- Pregnancy: weeks 3–8 organogenesis; thalidomide, isotretinoin, valproate, warfarin; FDA letters replaced by PLLR in 2015.
- Lactation: weak bases trapped in milk; relative infant dose under about 10%.
- Elderly: polypharmacy, renal decline, falls; Beers and STOPP/START.
- CIOMS (1949, WHO + UNESCO); CIOMS I form; working groups I–X.
- CDSCO/DCGI; D&C Act 1940, Rules 1945; Schedule Y 2005 → NDCT Rules 2019; PSUR 6-monthly × 2 years then annual × 2 years.
